title: Coastal flooding warning for Metro Vancouver as king tides coincide with storms across coastal B.C.
summary: Many coastal communities of B.C. are preparing with sandbags and clearing debris as a king tide coincides with waves of heavy rain and wind on Wednesday.

image.caption: High tides are seen in Delta's Boundary Bay on Tuesday. King tides are coinciding with storms hitting coastal B.C. through the middle of the week, with communities like Delta preparing with sandbags. (Hunter Soo/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Many coastal communities of B.C. are preparing with sandbags and clearing debris as a king tide coincides with waves of heavy rain and wind on Wednesday.
Warnings cover swath of coastal B.C. as storms batter region, communities prepared with sandbags

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) issued an orange coastal flooding warning for Metro Vancouver, with yellow coastal flooding warnings in place for the entirety of Vancouver Island, most of Haida Gwaii and parts of the Central Coast.
The forecaster said storm surges would lead to water levels 0.4 to 0.7 metres higher than usual on Wednesday and Thursday, saying it would lead to "moderate to significant coastal flooding."
Some Vancouver Island communities, including the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and Parksville, issued evacuation alerts for low-lying areas as they prepared for the high tides to hit.

Environment Canada has UPGRADED the Coastal Flooding Statement to a Coastal Flooding Warning for multiple #BC coastline areas. Stay away from affected coastlines &amp; use caution in low lying areas. Learn more: https://t.co/jjChhib25Q #BCStorm #BC https://t.co/ZMovroKIbd—EmergencyInfoBC
In Metro Vancouver, the City of Delta said earlier this week it was "taking proactive steps to prepare low-lying coastal neighbourhoods for flood mitigation and response."
The Nuu-chah-nulth First Nation community of Ahousaht, near Tofino, declared a state of local emergency due to the storm as water ate away at the shoreline.
ECCC said coastal erosion was likely in sensitive areas, and forecasters are saying that people should move valuables and toxic chemicals from basements to elevated locations.
B.C. Ferries cancelled a number of evening sailings between Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island, citing high winds in the Strait of Georgia.

#ServiceNotice To ensure the safety of our customers and crew, the following sailings between #Tsawwassen and #SwartzBay must be cancelled for tonight as a result of the severe weather forecast for high winds in the Strait of Georgia. Fore more: https://t.co/fiCkav7x8V https://t.co/CzeJCzqFYu—BCFerries
State of local emergency in Squamish
Meanwhile, in the Sea-to-Sky region, a state of local emergency was put in place in Squamish, which was significantly affected by storms earlier this month.
Low-pressure system drenches Vancouver Island
Squamish Mayor Sean Easton said the high tides were going to combine with high water levels from those storms.
"As part of the state of emergency, we are taking proactive measures and doing sandbagging ... and doing impromptu or proactive diking," he said late Tuesday.
Easton said the district was paying close attention to certain areas that were affected by king tides in 2022, and was particularly helping unhoused residents living in an encampment along waterways.
"It's an example of these extreme weather events really impacting directly, in this case, marginalized communities," he said.
The district said people should stay clear of rivers and not drive across flooded roads, as the B.C. River Forecast Centre issued high streamflow advisories for Vancouver Island and the South Coast.
Flood watch

A flood watch was issued for Eastern Vancouver Island on Wednesday, saying that warm temperatures accompanying the storm may result to rain falling on snow, which could worsen runoff and increase river flows.
ECCC said that Wednesday evening will see the final storm in a "series of potent weather systems" that battered the B.C. coast all week.
Highway 16 on Haida Gwaii was closed on Tuesday due to debris and water on the road, according to DriveBC. (DriveBC)

The Transportation Ministry said in a Tuesday traffic advisory that communities along Highway 101 on the Sunshine Coast and Howe Sound, as well as those along the Malahat Highway and on the west coast of Vancouver Island, were likely to be most affected by the incoming weather.
Other communities on Vancouver Island, like Tofino and Ucluelet, said public beach access would be closed due to the incoming storms.

items: How king tides happen, and what that means amid flood warnings in B.C.

blocks.text: A king tide refers to a phenomenon where cosmic alignments can mean dramatic tides, which can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average high tide mark.

The current king tide is expected to end on Thursday, but up until then, officials are warning people along the coast about the potential of flooding, as these higher-than-normal tides coincide with sea level rise caused by El Niño.
